title: Python deeper
summary: Modules, classes, iteration, decorators, closures and typing.

lessons.title: Modules and imports
lessons.body:
# Modules and imports

Every `.py` file is a module. A folder of modules is a package. `import` runs a module's top-level code once, caches it in `sys.modules`, and gives you a name for it.

```python
import math
import json as js
from collections import Counter

print(math.pi)
print(js.dumps({"a": 1}))
print(Counter("aab"))
```

## Where Python looks

Python searches the folders in `sys.path`: the script's folder, then the standard library, then installed packages. A file named `random.py` next to your script hides the real `random`, so avoid names of standard modules.

## The main guard

```python
def main():
    print("running")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

A module's `__name__` is `"__main__"` only when it runs as a script, so importing this file will not start `main`. Prefer `import x` over `from x import *`, so readers can see where every name came from.
lessons.task: Import from the standard library at the top of the file. Write `circle_area(r)` using `math.pi`. Write `most_common_word(words)` using `from collections import Counter`, returning the most frequent word (first seen wins a tie) or `None` for an empty list. Write `to_json(data)` returning JSON text with sorted keys.

checks.name: uses math.pi
checks.code:
import math
assert math.isclose(circle_area(2), math.pi * 4), circle_area(2)

checks.name: imports Counter by name
checks.code:
from collections import Counter as real_counter
assert globals().get("Counter") is real_counter, "use: from collections import Counter"

checks.name: most common word
checks.code:
got = most_common_word(["a", "b", "b", "c"])
assert got == "b", got

checks.name: ties and empty lists
checks.code:
got = most_common_word(["x", "y", "y", "x"])
assert got == "x", got
assert most_common_word([]) is None, most_common_word([])

checks.name: JSON with sorted keys
checks.code:
got = to_json({"b": 1, "a": [True, None]})
assert got == '{"a": [true, null], "b": 1}', got

hints: All three tools come from the standard library: `math`, `collections` and `json`. Your imports go at the top.
`Counter(words).most_common(1)` returns a list holding one `(word, count)` pair. `json.dumps` has a `sort_keys` argument.
`Counter(words).most_common(1)[0][0]` after handling the empty list, and `json.dumps(data, sort_keys=True)`.
lessons.explanation:
`most_common` orders equal counts by first appearance, so ties resolve predictably without extra code.

`import math` keeps the module name visible at the call site. `from collections import Counter` is reasonable when one name is used often and its origin is obvious.

lessons.title: Classes
lessons.body:
# Classes

A class bundles data with the functions that work on it. Each object, or instance, has its own attributes.

```python
class Dog:
    legs = 4  # shared by all dogs

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name  # per dog

    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name}: woof"

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"Dog({self.name!r})"
```

`__init__` sets up a new object. `self` is that object, and Python passes it for you when you call `rex.speak()`. `__repr__` controls how the object appears when printed in a list or a debugger.

## Inheritance

```python
class Puppy(Dog):
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        super().__init__(name)
        self.age = age
```

`Puppy` gets every `Dog` method and can add or replace them. `super()` calls the parent version. Keep hierarchies shallow. Often a plain function or a stored object is simpler.
lessons.task: Write `Wallet(owner, balance=0)` with `deposit(amount)` and `withdraw(amount)`, each returning the new balance and raising `ValueError` for a non-positive amount or, for `withdraw`, too little money. Its repr is `Wallet('Ada', 10)`. Write `SavingsWallet(Wallet)` taking `rate=0.1`, with `add_interest()` adding `balance * rate`.

checks.name: deposit and withdraw
checks.code:
w = Wallet("Ada")
assert w.balance == 0, w.balance
assert w.deposit(10) == 10, w.balance
assert w.withdraw(3) == 7, w.balance

checks.name: rejects bad amounts
can withdraw everything
checks.code:
w = Wallet("Ada", 5)
assert w.withdraw(5) == 0, w.balance

checks.name: repr
checks.code: assert repr(Wallet("Ada", 10)) == "Wallet('Ada', 10)", repr(Wallet("Ada", 10))

checks.name: wallets are independent
checks.code:
a = Wallet("A")
b = Wallet("B")
a.deposit(5)
assert b.balance == 0, b.balance

checks.name: savings wallet inherits and adds interest
checks.code:
s = SavingsWallet("Bo", 100, rate=0.5)
assert isinstance(s, Wallet), type(s).__mro__
s.add_interest()
assert s.balance == 150, s.balance
assert s.deposit(50) == 200, s.balance
assert SavingsWallet("Bo").rate == 0.1, SavingsWallet("Bo").rate

hints: Store `balance` on `self` in `__init__`. Everything else reads and updates `self.balance`.
Validate first and change the balance after, so a failed call leaves it untouched. In the subclass, call `super().__init__(owner, balance)`.
`if amount > self.balance: raise ValueError("not enough money")`. For the repr: `f"Wallet({self.owner!r}, {self.balance})"`. In `add_interest`: `self.balance += self.balance * self.rate`.
lessons.explanation:
Validating before changing state means a raised error leaves the object as it was. That is the easiest invariant to keep.

`!r` in the f-string uses `repr`, which adds the quotes around the owner name. The subclass reuses parent setup through `super()` instead of repeating it, so a later change to `Wallet` reaches both classes.

lessons.title: Dataclasses
lessons.body:
# Dataclasses

`@dataclass` writes `__init__`, `__repr__` and `__eq__` from a list of annotated fields. Use it for objects that mainly hold data.

```python
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass
class Order:
    item: str
    qty: int = 1
    notes: list[str] = field(
        default_factory=list)
```

Each `Order` gets its own `notes` list. A plain `notes: list = []` is rejected with an error, because all instances would share one list.

## Options

- `frozen=True` makes instances immutable and hashable, so they can be dict keys.
- `order=True` adds `<`, `>` and friends, comparing fields in order.
- `slots=True` uses less memory and blocks stray attributes.

## Validation

`__post_init__` runs right after the generated `__init__`:

```python
@dataclass
class Age:
    years: int

    def __post_init__(self):
        if self.years < 0:
            raise ValueError("negative")
```
lessons.task: Write a dataclass `Task` with `title: str`, `priority: int = 0` and `tags: list[str]` defaulting to a new empty list, raising `ValueError` for an empty title. Write a frozen dataclass `Point` with `x: int` and `y: int`.

checks.name: Task is a dataclass with defaults
checks.code:
import dataclasses
assert dataclasses.is_dataclass(Task), "use @dataclass"
t = Task("write")
assert (t.title, t.priority, t.tags) == ("write", 0, []), t

checks.name: compares by value
checks.code:
assert Task("a", 1) == Task("a", 1), "equal fields should compare equal"
assert Task("a", 1) != Task("a", 2), "different fields should differ"

checks.name: tags are not shared
checks.code:
a = Task("a")
b = Task("b")
a.tags.append("x")
assert b.tags == [], b.tags

checks.name: rejects an empty title
Point is frozen
checks.code:
import dataclasses
p = Point(1, 2)
assert (p.x, p.y) == (1, 2), p
raised = False
try:
    p.x = 5
except dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError:
    raised = True
assert raised, "assigning to a frozen Point should raise"

checks.name: Point is hashable
checks.code:
assert {Point(1, 2): "a"}[Point(1, 2)] == "a", "equal points should find the same key"
assert len({Point(0, 0), Point(0, 0), Point(0, 1)}) == 2, "sets should drop equal points"

hints: Import `dataclass` and `field` from `dataclasses`, and put the annotated fields directly in the class body.
A list default needs `field(default_factory=list)`. Validation goes in `__post_init__`, and `@dataclass(frozen=True)` handles `Point`.
`tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)`, then `def __post_init__(self): if not self.title: raise ValueError("title is required")`.
lessons.explanation:
`default_factory` runs once per instance, so tags are never shared. Dataclasses refuse a bare mutable default because it would be a bug in nearly every case.

Freezing a dataclass with the default `eq=True` also generates `__hash__`. That is what lets `Point` work as a dict key. Hash and equality must agree, and frozen fields cannot change, so they always will.

lessons.title: Protocols and duck typing
lessons.body:
# Protocols and duck typing

Python does not ask what class an object is. It asks whether the object has the attribute you are about to use. That is duck typing: if it has `.read()`, it can be read.

```python
def shout(thing):
    return thing.text().upper()
```

Any object with a `text` method works, and no shared base class is needed.

## Writing the contract down

`typing.Protocol` names the shape you expect, so type checkers can verify it. Classes do not inherit from it.

```python
from typing import Protocol
from typing import runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class HasText(Protocol):
    def text(self) -> str: ...

class Note:
    def text(self):
        return "hi"

isinstance(Note(), HasText)  # True
```

`runtime_checkable` allows `isinstance`, but it only checks that the method name exists. It does not look at parameters or return types.
lessons.task: Write a runtime-checkable protocol `Renderer` with `render(self) -> str`. Write classes `Text(value)` rendering the value and `Bold(value)` rendering `**value**`, neither inheriting from `Renderer`. Write `render_all(items)` joining the rendered items with newlines.

checks.name: renders each class
checks.code:
assert Text("a").render() == "a", Text("a").render()
assert Bold("a").render() == "**a**", Bold("a").render()

checks.name: joins with newlines
checks.code:
got = render_all([Text("a"), Bold("b")])
assert got == "a\n**b**", repr(got)
assert render_all([]) == "", render_all([])

checks.name: accepts any object with render
matches the protocol
checks.code:
assert isinstance(Text("a"), Renderer), "Text should match Renderer"
assert isinstance(Bold("a"), Renderer), "Bold should match Renderer"
assert not isinstance(3, Renderer), "an int has no render method"

checks.name: no inheritance needed
checks.code:
assert Renderer not in Text.__mro__, "Text should not inherit from Renderer"
assert Renderer not in Bold.__mro__, "Bold should not inherit from Renderer"

hints: A protocol is a class that inherits `Protocol`, with method bodies of `...`. Add `@runtime_checkable` above it.
`Text` and `Bold` each gain a `render` method. `render_all` only needs to call `.render()`, without checking types.
`class Renderer(Protocol):` with `def render(self) -> str: ...`, and `return "\n".join(i.render() for i in items)`.
lessons.explanation:
`render_all` never names a class, so it accepts anything with a `render` method, including classes written later.

A protocol adds a checkable contract without forcing a shared base class. Use one when you want tools to catch a missing method before the code runs. `isinstance` against a protocol only confirms the name exists, so it is not a full proof.

lessons.title: Iterators and generators
lessons.body:
# Iterators and generators

An iterable is anything `for` can walk. `iter(x)` gets an iterator from it, and `next(it)` returns one item at a time, raising `StopIteration` at the end. An iterator is used up once.

```python
it = iter([1, 2])
next(it)  # 1
next(it)  # 2
# next(it) would raise StopIteration
```

A class joins in by defining `__iter__`. If `__iter__` builds a fresh iterator each time, the object can be looped over repeatedly.

## Generators

A function containing `yield` returns a generator, which is an iterator that pauses at each `yield`. Values are made on demand, so sequences can be huge or endless.

```python
def evens():
    n = 0
    while True:
        yield n
        n += 2

def both(a, b):
    yield from a
    yield from b
```

`yield from` hands over to another iterable, which is ideal for recursive walks.
lessons.task: Write a class `Countdown(start)` whose instances can be looped over more than once, producing `start` down to 1. Write a generator function `flatten(items)` yielding every non-list value from arbitrarily nested lists.

checks.name: counts down
checks.code:
assert list(Countdown(3)) == [3, 2, 1], list(Countdown(3))
assert list(Countdown(0)) == [], list(Countdown(0))

checks.name: can be looped twice
checks.code:
c = Countdown(2)
assert list(c) == [2, 1], "first loop"
assert list(c) == [2, 1], "second loop should start again"

checks.name: follows the iterator protocol
checks.code:
it = iter(Countdown(1))
assert next(it) == 1, "first value"
raised = False
try:
    next(it)
except StopIteration:
    raised = True
assert raised, "an exhausted iterator should raise StopIteration"

checks.name: flattens any depth
checks.code:
got = list(flatten([1, [2, [3, [4]]], 5]))
assert got == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], got
assert list(flatten([[], [[]]])) == [], list(flatten([[], [[]]]))

checks.name: strings stay whole
checks.code:
got = list(flatten(["ab", ["cd"]]))
assert got == ["ab", "cd"], got

checks.name: flatten is a lazy generator
checks.code:
import inspect
assert inspect.isgeneratorfunction(flatten), "flatten should use yield"
assert next(flatten([1, [2]])) == 1, "first value"

hints: If `__iter__` contains `yield`, every call to it gets a fresh generator with its own position.
In `flatten`, check `isinstance(item, list)`. A list needs another call to `flatten`, and anything else is yielded as it is.
`def __iter__(self):` with a local `n = self.start` and `while n > 0: yield n; n -= 1`. Then `yield from flatten(item)` for lists and `yield item` otherwise.
lessons.explanation:
Counting in a local variable inside `__iter__` keeps the position out of the object, so two loops over one `Countdown` cannot interfere.

`yield from flatten(item)` passes along everything the inner call produces. A generator holds one frame per nesting level, so memory use follows the depth rather than the number of items.

lessons.title: Context managers
lessons.body:
# Context managers

`with` guarantees cleanup, whichever way a block ends. An object supports it by defining `__enter__` and `__exit__`.

```python
class Timer:
    def __enter__(self):
        return self

    def __exit__(self, kind, err, tb):
        print("done")
        return False  # do not swallow
```

`__exit__` receives details of any exception. A true return value suppresses it, so usually return `False`.

## The short form

`contextlib.contextmanager` turns a generator into a context manager. Code before `yield` is the setup. Code after it is the cleanup.

```python
from contextlib import contextmanager

@contextmanager
def tag(out, name):
    out.append(f"<{name}>")
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        out.append(f"</{name}>")
```

The `try`/`finally` matters. An exception inside the `with` block is raised at the `yield`, so without `finally` your cleanup would be skipped.
lessons.task: Write a context manager `temporary_setting(settings, key, value)` that sets `settings[key] = value` for the block, then restores the old value, or removes the key if it did not exist before. It must clean up after an exception and let the exception propagate.

checks.name: sets the value inside the block
restores the old value
checks.code:
s = {"debug": False}
with temporary_setting(s, "debug", True):
    pass
assert s == {"debug": False}, s

checks.name: removes a key that was absent
checks.code:
s = {}
with temporary_setting(s, "debug", True):
    assert s == {"debug": True}, s
assert s == {}, s

checks.name: a stored None still counts as present
checks.code:
s = {"mode": None}
with temporary_setting(s, "mode", "fast"):
    pass
assert s == {"mode": None}, s

checks.name: cleans up after an exception
nests correctly
checks.code:
s = {"n": 1}
with temporary_setting(s, "n", 2):
    with temporary_setting(s, "n", 3):
        assert s["n"] == 3, s
    assert s["n"] == 2, s
assert s["n"] == 1, s

hints: Before changing anything, record what is there now. You need to know whether the key existed and what its value was.
`None` could be a real stored value, so `key in settings` is the reliable test. Wrap the `yield` in `try`/`finally`.
`had_key = key in settings`, `old = settings.get(key)`, set the value, then `try: yield`, and `finally:` restore `old` if `had_key`, otherwise `del settings[key]`.
lessons.explanation:
An exception raised in the `with` block appears at the `yield`, so `finally` is what guarantees restoration. No `except` means the exception keeps travelling to the caller.

Testing `key in settings` separately from reading the value keeps "missing" distinct from "stored as `None`".

lessons.title: Decorators
lessons.task: Write a decorator `count_calls` that stores how many times the function ran in a `.calls` attribute, starting at 0. Write a decorator factory `retry(times)` that calls the function up to `times` times in total, returning the first success and re-raising the last exception if all fail. Both keep the function's name.

checks.name: counts calls
checks.code:
@count_calls
def add(a, b=0):
    return a + b
assert add.calls == 0, add.calls
assert add(1, b=2) == 3, "should pass arguments through"
add(1)
assert add.calls == 2, add.calls

checks.name: keeps the name
counters are separate
retries until success
gives up and re-raises
does not retry after success
checks.code:
attempts = []
@retry(5)
def fine():
    attempts.append(1)
    return "ok"
assert fine() == "ok", "return value"
assert len(attempts) == 1, attempts

hints: Functions are objects, so you can set `wrapper.calls = 0` before returning `wrapper`, and add to it inside.
`retry` has three layers: `retry(times)`, `decorator(fn)`, `wrapper(*args, **kwargs)`. The wrapper loops, and `return` inside `try` stops on the first success.
`for attempt in range(times):`, `try: return fn(*args, **kwargs)`, `except Exception:` and `if attempt == times - 1: raise`.
lessons.explanation:
Storing the count on the wrapper gives each decorated function its own counter, reachable from outside.

In `retry`, a bare `raise` inside `except` re-raises the current exception with its original traceback. Catching `Exception` leaves `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit` alone, so a stop request is never retried.

lessons.title: Functions that return functions
lessons.body:
# Functions that return functions

A function defined inside another can read the outer function's variables. When the inner function is returned, it keeps those variables alive. That pairing is a closure.

```python
def make_adder(n):
    def add(x):
        return x + n
    return add

add_two = make_adder(2)
add_two(3)  # 5
```

Each call to `make_adder` creates a new `n`, so closures from separate calls do not interfere.

## Changing a captured variable

Reading works automatically. Assigning would make a new local variable, so declare the name with `nonlocal` first:

```python
def counter():
    count = 0
    def tick():
        nonlocal count
        count += 1
        return count
    return tick
```

Closures give you small pieces of private state without a class. Reach for a class when you need several methods or want other code to inspect that state.
lessons.task: Write `running_total()` returning a function `add(n)`. Each call adds `n` to a total kept inside the closure and returns the new total. Separate calls to `running_total()` keep separate totals.
lessons.solution:
def running_total():
    total = 0

    def add(n):
        nonlocal total
        total += n
        return total

    return add

checks.name: adds up
checks.code:
add = running_total()
assert add(5) == 5, "first call"
assert add(3) == 8, "second call"
assert add(-2) == 6, "third call"

checks.name: adding zero keeps the total
checks.code:
add = running_total()
add(4)
assert add(0) == 4, "adding 0"

checks.name: totals are independent
checks.code:
a = running_total()
b = running_total()
a(10)
assert b(1) == 1, "b should not see a's total"
assert a(1) == 11, "a should keep its own total"

checks.name: state lives in the closure
checks.code:
add = running_total()
add(1)
assert add.__closure__, "add should capture total from running_total"

hints: The total has to be created inside `running_total`, so each call gets its own.
Assigning to `total` inside `add` makes Python treat it as local, which raises `UnboundLocalError`. One keyword fixes that.
Inside `running_total`: `total = 0`, then `def add(n):` with `nonlocal total`, `total += n`, `return total`. Finally `return add`.
lessons.explanation:
Each call to `running_total` runs its body once, creating a new `total` and a new `add` bound to it. The function object carries a reference to that variable in `__closure__`, which is why the value survives after `running_total` returns.

`nonlocal` tells Python that the assignment targets the enclosing variable. A module-level total would be shared by every counter.

lessons.title: Typing
lessons.body:
# Typing

Annotations describe what a function expects. Python does not enforce them at runtime. Tools such as type checkers and editors read them, and so do people.

```python
def lengths(
    words: list[str],
) -> dict[str, int]:
    return {w: len(w) for w in words}
```

- `list[str]`, `dict[str, int]` and `tuple[int, int]` describe contents.
- `int | None` means either one.
- `type UserId = int` creates a named alias.

## Generic functions

A type parameter links an input type to an output type:

```python
def last[T](items: list[T]) -> T:
    return items[-1]
```

Now a checker knows that `last(["a"])` is a `str`.

## Lazy annotations

Since Python 3.14, annotations are evaluated only when something asks for them, so a class can name itself in its own methods without quotes. `typing.get_type_hints(fn)` returns the evaluated annotations.
lessons.task: Add exact annotations: `word_lengths(words: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]`, and make `first_or_none` generic with a type parameter `T`, taking `items: list[T]` and returning `T | None`. Define the alias `type Scores = dict[str, int]`. Fix `first_or_none` so that it returns `None` for an empty list.

checks.name: word_lengths annotations
checks.code:
import typing
hints = typing.get_type_hints(word_lengths)
assert hints == {"words": list[str], "return": dict[str, int]}, hints

checks.name: word_lengths still works
checks.code: assert word_lengths(["ab", "c"]) == {"ab": 2, "c": 1}, word_lengths(["ab", "c"])

checks.name: first_or_none is generic
checks.code:
import typing
params = first_or_none.__type_params__
assert len(params) == 1, "use def first_or_none[T](...)"
T = params[0]
hints = typing.get_type_hints(first_or_none)
assert hints == {"items": list[T], "return": T | None}, hints

checks.name: first_or_none behaviour
checks.code:
assert first_or_none([3, 4]) == 3, first_or_none([3, 4])
assert first_or_none([]) is None, first_or_none([])
assert first_or_none([0]) == 0, first_or_none([0])

checks.name: Scores alias
checks.code:
import typing
assert isinstance(Scores, typing.TypeAliasType), "use: type Scores = dict[str, int]"
assert Scores.__value__ == dict[str, int], Scores.__value__

hints: Start with the annotation on `word_lengths`, which is written out in the task. Then handle the empty case of `first_or_none`.
A type parameter goes in square brackets after the function name, as in `def f[T](...)`. The alias uses the `type` statement.
`def first_or_none[T](items: list[T]) -> T | None:` with `return items[0] if items else None`, and `type Scores = dict[str, int]`.
lessons.explanation:
Annotations do not change how the code runs, which is why the empty-list bug needed a real fix. They do let a checker warn callers that the result might be `None`.

The type parameter ties the element type to the return type. `items[0] if items else None` tests whether the list is empty rather than whether its first value is falsy, so `[0]` still returns `0`.
